stem: Which method returns the first element in the document that matches a CSS selector?

options.text: `document.querySelector()`
options.why: It takes any CSS selector and returns the first match, or null.

options.text: `document.querySelectorAll()`
options.why: It returns a NodeList of every match, not just the first.

options.text: `document.getElementsByClassName()`
options.why: It matches class names only and returns a live collection.

options.text: `document.getElementById()`
options.why: It only looks up elements by id, not by arbitrary selectors.

explanation: `querySelector` accepts any CSS selector (`#id`, `.class`, `[data-x]`, combinators) and returns the first matching element or `null`.

stem: Calling `event.stopPropagation()` in a link's click handler also stops the browser from following the link.

options.text: True
options.why: stopPropagation only stops the event from reaching other elements' listeners.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: preventing the default action is preventDefault's job.

explanation: `stopPropagation()` halts bubbling and capturing; `preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action. They are independent, and you can call both.

stem: A list gains hundreds of `<li>` items at runtime. What is the most efficient way to handle clicks on any item?

options.text: Add a click listener to each `<li>` as it is created
options.why: It works, but costs a listener per item and needs cleanup when items are removed.

options.text: Add one listener to the parent `<ul>` and find the item with `event.target.closest('li')`
options.why: Event delegation uses bubbling so a single listener covers current and future items.

options.text: Use inline `onclick` attributes in the HTML strings
options.why: Inline handlers mix markup and code and are blocked by strict Content Security Policies.

options.text: Poll the list with `setInterval` every 100 ms, looking for new items and attaching listeners to each
options.why: Polling wastes work and still leaves gaps between checks.

explanation: Event delegation relies on clicks bubbling up to an ancestor. One listener handles every item, including ones added later.

stem: Match each event with when it fires.

options.text: The HTML is parsed and the DOM is built (images may still be loading)
The page and all its resources have finished loading
On every change to a text field's value
When a text field's changed value is committed, for example on blur
When an element scrolls into view

explanation: Use `DOMContentLoaded` to start scripts that need the DOM, `input` for live updates, and `change` for committed values. No event fires on scrolling into view; that is what IntersectionObserver is for.

stem: In the search box case study, which two changes reliably stop stale results from showing? (Choose two.)

options.text: Debounce the input handler so it runs 250 ms after typing stops
options.why: Debouncing reduces requests, but a slow earlier response can still land after a faster later one.

options.text: Abort the previous request with an `AbortController` before sending a new one
options.why: An aborted fetch rejects, so the stale response is never rendered.

options.text: Tag each request with an increasing id and ignore any response that is not the latest
options.why: Checking the id before rendering guarantees only the newest query's results appear.

options.text: Switch from `fetch` to `XMLHttpRequest`
options.why: The transport doesn't matter; responses can still arrive out of order.

options.text: Use `await` instead of `.then()` to handle the response
options.why: await is only syntax; it does not change which response renders last.

explanation: Either cancel superseded requests or discard responses that are no longer current. Debouncing is a good addition for load, but on its own it doesn't remove the race.

stem: Which storage keeps data after the user closes the tab and comes back to the site days later?

options.text: `sessionStorage`
options.why: sessionStorage is cleared when the tab (page session) ends.

options.text: `localStorage`
options.why: localStorage persists per origin until it is cleared by the site or the user.

options.text: A global JavaScript variable
options.why: Variables live only as long as the page is open.

options.text: `history.state`
options.why: History state belongs to a session history entry, not long-term storage.

explanation: `localStorage` survives restarts; `sessionStorage` lasts for one tab session. Both store strings only and are synchronous, so keep them small.

stem: How do you cancel an in-flight `fetch` request?

options.text: Call `fetch.cancel()` with the request URL
options.why: fetch has no cancel method.

options.text: Reject the returned promise yourself
options.why: Code outside a promise cannot reject it, and doing so would not stop the network request.

options.text: Pass an `AbortController`'s `signal` to `fetch`, then call `controller.abort()`
options.why: Aborting the signal cancels the request and rejects the fetch promise with an AbortError.

options.text: Set a `timeout` option on the request so the browser abandons it after the delay
options.why: fetch has no timeout option; use AbortSignal.timeout() to build a signal instead.

explanation: `const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal }); c.abort();` For deadlines, `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })`.

stem: `fetch` only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP errors like 404. Which boolean property of the `Response` is `true` only for status codes 200–299? Type the property name.
explanation: Check `if (!response.ok) throw new Error(response.status)` after every fetch; otherwise a 404 or 500 page looks like success.

stem: You can store an object in `localStorage` and get the same object back later without any conversion.

options.text: True
options.why: Values are converted to strings; an object becomes the text "[object Object]".

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: serialise with JSON.stringify and parse it back with JSON.parse.

explanation: Web Storage only stores strings. Round-trip objects with `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse`, and wrap access in `try/catch` because storage can be unavailable.

stem: Which statements about `IntersectionObserver` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It reports when an observed element enters or leaves the viewport or a chosen root element
options.why: That visibility change is exactly what it observes.

options.text: It is an efficient replacement for scroll listeners when lazy-loading images
options.why: The browser computes intersections off the main scroll path and batches the callbacks.

options.text: It runs its callback synchronously on every scroll event
options.why: Callbacks are asynchronous and fire only when an intersection threshold is crossed.

options.text: Each observer can watch only one element
options.why: One observer can observe any number of elements.

options.text: It needs a third-party library to work
options.why: It is a built-in browser API.

explanation: Use `IntersectionObserver` for lazy loading, infinite scroll and "seen" tracking instead of measuring elements in scroll handlers.
